voiceover: This isn't a believer's story about Jesus. It's an enemy's confession. In his own hand, Saul of Tarsus wrote that he persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. He had every earthly reason not to switch sides — status, a career, his safety — and he burned all of it, escaping one city lowered in a basket through a hole in the wall. And the easy explanations don't fit him. He wasn't grieving Jesus. He wasn't hoping Jesus was alive — he thought the movement was blasphemy worth killing for. He wasn't swept along by the group — he was leading the other side. But here's the part most people never hear. He didn't just believe it. He went and cross-examined the other witnesses: fifteen days with Peter, then with James — the very men who said they saw Jesus alive. And it's early — Paul's letters come before the Gospels, and the creed he quotes dates to within a few years of the cross. Even atheist scholars grant that dating. Christianity's fiercest destroyer became its boldest witness. Not a fan. Not a follower. This is the enemy's own confession: he had met the risen Jesus.
